items.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: He would sit over there and look at me and he’d say “go on, Purdie, go on, Purdie.” And we’d just groove. We instantly hit it off, the first time that we were doing demos.

ctx.x: Exactly. And that’s what I was doing and I didn’t know it. And that’s where my mouth got me into trouble. And that’s why I’m talking about being a big mouth. I will be the first one to jump up and tell the arranger and the producer and the writer that you’re

wrong. And the part that hurts the most is that I was always right. They did not like it and I can’t blame them. I mean it took me years to understand that, but the point was was that I just had this instinct. And I had it all my life, to make things work. Just make it work. Always thinking about making it work. Putting things together. I could always put things together. I could always put people together. I could always put places together. I could always. I mean I was a natural leader. But I was a great…
Rock & roll type demos? R&B things?

items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: then we add drums, either Bernard Purdie or Dennis Mackrel or Joe Cocuzzo

ctx.x: And these days, you split your time between going around to these jazz parties and doing recording. Have you got a recording session planned coming up?

No the only records we make now for companies that want to make a jazz record like Arbors or the company I used to be with, LRC Records with New York Swing, it’s John Bunch and Jay Leonhart, just a trio, and then we add drums, either Bernard Purdie or Dennis Mackrel or Joe Cocuzzo. But we found out that it works better on the road with just three, without the drums.

items.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015
items.q: So we used him on a record date, John and I.

ctx.x: I don’t know, he gave me the impression that you helped him not get in trouble.

Yeah, well, in other words, when I heard him play on a ship he was playing in a jam session one night. I said, “who the hell is that drummer?” It was Pretty Purdie. And he was swinging. So we used him on a record date, John and I. He played “Sing Sing Sing” — it was unbelievable. He knew it backwards.
All right, I’m going to try another tune on you here. I’m just going to give you —
